---
title: "Research"
---

My research is about **informal employment**: why workers hold jobs without a
contract or social security, what they give up by doing so, and what actually
changes when they become formal. I combine large household panel surveys with
structural search models. A second strand, from my time at the IDB, looks at
fiscal rules and sovereign debt in emerging economies.

## Job Market Paper

::: {.paper}
::: {.paper-title}
Wages, amenities and the value of a formal job: A structural approach for Mexico
:::
::: {.paper-meta}
Sole authored · Draft, 2026
:::

In Mexico, most workers who move from informal to formal employment never
change employer — the firm they already work for simply registers them. This
paper asks what that formal status is worth, given that the wage gain is small.

<details class="abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<div class="abstract-body">
In Mexico most moves from informal to formal employment happen without a change
of employer: the same firm registers a worker it already employs. Using the
rotating panel of the National Survey of Occupation and Employment (2005–2025),
I show that 77% of informal-to-formal transitions take place within the firm and
that such formalisation raises hourly wages by only about 5%. The gain accrues
to low-skilled workers even though skilled workers formalise at higher rates,
which suggests that workers accept formal status for reasons beyond the wage. I
estimate a two-sector search model that decomposes the value of a formal job
into the formal-sector amenity, future job opportunities and job stability, and
in which formal offers reach informal workers both from outside firms and from
their current employer — a foot in the door to formality. The estimated amenity
is worth 29.4% of the median informal wage to skilled men and 15.2% to skilled
women, is negative for low-skilled women, and cannot be distinguished from zero
for low-skilled men. The foot-in-the-door channel is worth a further 4 to 16% of
the median informal wage, and it cuts both ways: because a worker can wait to be
registered in place, the same channel that supplies most entries into formality
also raises the value of staying informal. Closing it lowers formal employment
by 8 to 14 percentage points among men, part of that through withdrawal from
employment rather than a move into informal work.
</div>
</details>

*JEL:* J24, J31, J46, J64, O17<br>
*Keywords:* informal employment, search frictions, compensating differentials

Draft available on request.
:::

## Work in Progress

::: {.paper}
::: {.paper-title}
The wage growth penalty of informal employment
:::
::: {.paper-meta}
Sole authored · Estimates complete, draft in preparation
:::

Do informal jobs not only pay less, but also grow more slowly? I estimate
life-cycle wage profiles separately by formality status, using the
Hause–Lillard–Topel approach together with an Oaxaca decomposition to separate
differences in returns to experience from differences in worker composition.
:::
